title: Moving to Florida? Why December 31, 2026 Matters for Your Taxes
dek: Amendment 3 raises the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, but only right away for people who are Florida residents by December 31. Here is what counts, who qualifies and what waiting costs.
body:
If you plan to move to Florida, being a permanent Florida resident by December 31, 2026 decides how soon you get the state's much bigger homestead exemption. Residents by that date get the larger exemption as soon as they own a home, live in it and file. People who become residents on January 1, 2027 or later start with the old, smaller exemption and wait until their fifth year of homestead for the bigger one.

You do not have to own a house by December 31. The test is where you permanently live, not when you close. That means renters can qualify, which surprises a lot of people.

What Amendment 3 changed

Florida voters approved Amendment 3 on November 3, 2026 with about 62% of the vote, just over the 60% it needed. It takes effect January 1, 2027.

Tax yearHomestead exemption on taxes other than school taxes
2026 (now)up to about $51,411 in total ($25,000 for all taxes plus $26,411 for non school taxes)
2027up to $150,000
2028up to $250,000
2029 onadjusted each year for inflation

Two things the headlines skip. First, the bigger exemption does not touch school taxes. The first $25,000 stays the only exemption on the school part of your bill, so almost every homeowner still pays school taxes. Second, it does not change tax rates. Cities and counties can still raise or lower their rates, and flat fees for things like trash and stormwater are not reduced by any exemption.

Save Our Homes stays in place, so a homestead's assessed value still can't rise more than 3% a year or inflation, whichever is less, and portability still works when you move from one Florida homestead to another.

What does it save in real dollars?

It depends on your county's rates and your home's assessed value, and nobody can give an exact number until the Legislature passes the rules that put the amendment in place. Several property appraisers have published estimates for a home that gets the full new exemption, using their county's average rate for everything except schools:

WhereAverage non school rateExtra savings in 2027Extra savings in 2028
Pinellas County (St. Petersburg, Clearwater, Dunedin)12.20 millsabout $1,203about $2,423
Volusia County (Daytona Beach, Ormond Beach, New Smyrna Beach, Port Orange)11.81 millsabout $1,164about $2,345
Broward County (Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood)not publishedabout $1,300 for the average homeownerabout $2,300
Florida average (Florida TaxWatch)10.50 millsabout $1,035about $2,085

The math is simple enough to do for your own county: the extra exempt value ($98,589 in 2027 and $198,589 in 2028, compared with today's exemption) times your non school millage rate divided by 1,000. Homes with an assessed value below the new exemption save less, because there is less value to exempt. Use your county property appraiser's estimator once it is updated.

What if I move after December 31?

You still get a homestead exemption, just the old size at first: about $50,000 on non school taxes, adjusted for inflation starting in 2028. You become eligible for the larger exemption starting January 1 of your fifth year of homestead. One law firm's reading, from Holland and Knight, is that years spent renting after the cutoff do not count toward those five years, because the clock runs on years of exemption, not years in Florida.

Using Volusia's example, a family that arrives in early 2027 and buys right away could pay roughly $2,300 a year more for about four years than a neighbor who arrived in December 2026. That is our rough math from the county's numbers, before inflation adjustments and rate changes, so treat it as a ballpark.

What counts as being a Florida resident by December 31?

No single document settles it. Residency comes down to where you actually live and intend to stay, backed up by records made at the time. The steps lawyers and appraisers point to include:

  • Living in a Florida home, owned or rented, as your main home
  • Filing a Declaration of Domicile with your county clerk
  • Getting a Florida driver license and giving up the old one
  • Registering to vote and registering your cars in Florida
  • Moving your mail, banking, job records and tax return address to Florida
  • Enrolling your kids in Florida schools and putting utilities in your name
  • Ending any homestead or residency claim in the state you left

Paperwork alone is not enough if your life still looks like it is somewhere else. A Florida license while you spend most of December in Ohio is a weak case. The Legislature is expected to set a uniform way to prove December 31 residency, but as of late November no special session date had been set, and new legislative leaders said they would not rush it.

I'm renting first. Do I still qualify?

Generally yes. If Florida is genuinely your permanent home by December 31, 2026, you should get the larger exemption when you later buy, live in the home and apply. The usual rules still apply: you need title to the home, it has to be your permanent residence on January 1 of the tax year, and the application is due March 1. Keep your lease, utility bills and license dates in one folder, because the proof rules are still being written.

What about second homes and rentals?

Homes that don't get homestead, like a vacation condo or a rental, get a different change. Starting in 2027 their assessed value for non school taxes can rise at most 5% a year instead of 10%. School taxes stay tied to market value. If you plan to keep your home up north and buy a second place here, that is the part that applies to you, and the December 31 date does not.

Should I rush my move?

Only if it already made sense. If you were going to move in the spring anyway and can make Florida your real home in the next few weeks, the savings can be worth it. If moving now means two leases, a rushed job change or a December spent living mostly elsewhere, the paper trail may not hold up anyway. Also remember the exemption saves money on one bill. Insurance, flood risk and HOA or condo dues usually move a Florida budget more, which we cover in the six bills nobody puts on the listing.

We are not lawyers or tax advisors, and the implementing rules are still coming. Check with your county property appraiser and a Florida attorney or CPA before you make a move based on this date.

Sources: Volusia County Property Appraiser and Pinellas County Property Appraiser Amendment 3 FAQs (Nov 2026); Broward County Property Appraiser estimate as reported by NBC 6 (Oct 2026); Florida TaxWatch property tax resource center (Nov 2026); Holland and Knight, "New Homestead Exemption Raises Stakes for Establishing Florida Residency Before Year End" (Nov 2026); Florida Realtors (Nov 2026); WLRN (Nov 5, 2026); CBS News Miami and News Service of Florida (Nov 17, 2026).
faq: Do I have to own a Florida home by December 31, 2026 to get the bigger homestead exemption?
No. The cutoff is about being a permanent Florida resident by December 31, 2026, not owning property. Residents by that date get the larger exemption when they later buy, live in the home and file.
Can renters qualify for the Amendment 3 homestead exemption?
Generally yes. If Florida is genuinely your permanent home by December 31, 2026 while you rent, you should be eligible for the larger exemption once you buy and qualify a homestead.
What happens if I move to Florida in 2027?
You start with the existing exemption of about $50,000 on non school taxes and become eligible for the larger one starting January 1 of your fifth year of homestead.
No. The new exemption applies only to taxes other than school taxes. The first $25,000 remains the only exemption on the school portion of the bill.
When is the Florida homestead application due?
March 1 of the tax year. The home must be your permanent residence on January 1 of that year.
